chunks: "The problem is that an NFET needs its gate about 5 volts above its source, and its source is the switch node, which swings up to V in .
So I need a gate-drive supply that floats with the switch node.

The standard answer is a bootstrap: a gate driver whose supply pin is a capacitor C boot connected from the driver's BST pin to the switch node, charged through a Schottky diode from a 5 volts or 12 volts rail.
When the low side is on, SW is near ground and the cap charges to about the rail minus a diode drop.
When the high side turns on, SW rises, the cap's top plate rides up with it, and the driver holds the gate at V SW plus about 4. 6 volts.
To size the cap, I take the gate charge, say 12 nC, divide by the droop I can tolerate, about 0.
3 volts, which gives about 40 nanofarads, then use 100 nanofarads or more to cover derating and driver quiescent current.
Considerations: the cap only recharges when the low side or its body diode pulls SW low, so there's a minimum off-time and a maximum duty cycle.
At start-up into a pre-biased output the cap might never charge. SW undershoots below ground in dead time, so the driver pins need the right rating.
dv/dt can false-trigger the driver, so I want good common-mode immunity. A gate or boot resistor controls edge speed. And layout: cap right at the pins.
If I needed 100% duty I'd add a charge pump or use a PFET."
